newsitem.title: UK: Lehman sees UK rates at 9% unless taxes rise.
newsitem.headline: Lehman sees UK rates at 9% unless taxes rise.

text.p: Michael Dicks, a Lehman Brothers economist in London, said official UK interest rates could end up at 9.0 percent or more next year compared with 6.5 percent currently if the government did not raise taxes in next month's budget.
The arguments were strong for a fiscal tightening in Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown's first budget on July 2, he said.

"The consequences of failing to do so are that the Bank of England would likely need to raise interest rates dramatically more than is currently priced in," Dicks wrote in Lehman Brothers "Global Weekly Monitor."
"If the Chancellor decides to make absolutely no fiscal effort, we reckon that base rates could well end up above 9.0 percent."

Dicks said that if Brown tightened the policy stance by the equivalent of one percent of GDP -- around 7.0 billion pounds in tax rises or spending cuts -- base rates need not go as high, especially if the fiscal tightening was targeted at households.

A rise in base rates of two percentage points would have broadly the same long-term effect as a cut in government spending of around 2.5 percent of GDP -- either would ultimately reduce activity by about two percent.
"However, fiscal tightening kicks in much more quickly. It also delivers a bigger overall impact on prices and with no perverse short-term impact."

The Labour government has said its first budget will centre on a "welfare-to-work" programme to create jobs for 250,000 young long-term unemployed people. This will be funded by a "windfall" tax on the profits of privatised utility companies.
Brown has limited his room for manoeuvre by promising not to raise income tax rates and to live within tight public spending limits set by the previous Conservative government.
But economists say he has considerable scope to "tinker" with other taxes, exemptions and allowances to boost revenue.
